newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr hits 4-yr high, Tokyo stocks sink on bank worry.
newsitem.headline: Dlr hits 4-yr high, Tokyo stocks sink on bank worry.

text.p: The dollar and the pound jumped to multi-year highs against the yen on Wednesday, while Tokyo stocks pared early losses but ended lower on jitters about the health of some Japanese banks.

Dollar bulls rode a wave optimism over the greenback's future, spurred by a belief that the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations would do little more than call for stable currency markets when they meet in Berlin this weekend.
The dollar powered to a four-year high of 123.18 yen in afternoon trading, while sterling soared to 200 yen, its highest level since October 1992.
"The G7 meeting may end up with only a call for stability in currency rates, which means that a gradual dollar rise would be possible beyond the meeting," said one currency dealer.
Most regional currencies, including the Thai baht and the South Korean won, fell against the dollar, although central bank intervention in Seoul limited the South Korean currency's drop.

Japanese authorities reacted with apparent calm to the yen's latest slide. "An excessive weakening as well as a strengthening of the yen is undesirable," Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a parliamentary panel as the yen neared its four-year low.
"Stable currency rates are important for the management of our economy," he said, adding that Tokyo would keep close watch on the effects of the weak yen and take "appropriate steps".

The Tokyo stock market's key barometer, the 225-share Nikkei average, finished a hectic day down 128.36 points or 0.70 percent at 18,185.97 after trimming losses which took the index down more than two percent in morning trade.
Market pundits said the fall in share prices, sparked by renewed worries about Japan's bad debt-laden banking sector, helped undermine sentiment towards the already downtrodden yen.

Weak share prices and banking worries mean Japan's monetary authorities are unlikely to tighten credit soon. Japan's rock-bottom interest rates make its currency less attractive to investors than the pound and the dollar.
Share prices fell sharply in morning trade after rumours about the financial health of Nippon Credit Bank Ltd battered financial sector shares.

Nippon Credit said in a statement there was no cause for concern about its health, but the bank's share price finished the day down 35 yen at 181 yen, an all-time low. Other bank shares also suffered.

Concern about the slow pace of banks' efforts to clean up bad loans left from the collapse of the "bubble" of inflated Japanese asset prices early this decade has dampened enthusiasm for the institutions' shares since the year began.

"Nippon Credit shares fell below 200 yen to an all-time low, which ignited a bank sector sell-off led by futures early in the morning, and the sour mood continued throughout the day," said Akishige Ishikura, a Dai-ichi Securities analyst.

The news that Japan posted a bigger deficit in its trade balance in the first 20 days of January also lifted the dollar against the yen in the morning. Japan's trade gap is often in deficit in early January due to New Year holidays, but the data eased worries over an expected rise in Tokyo's trade surplus.

Japan's customs-cleared trade deficit rose 23.4 percent to 350.68 billion yen ($2.87 billion) in the first 20 days of January from a deficit of 284.28 billion yen ($2.33 billion) in the same period a year earlier.
